title: Mold and Mildew on Siding: How to Remove It for Good
description: Black streaks and green film on siding are living growth. Learn how to identify it, clean it safely, and keep it from returning in Florida humidity.
h1: Mold and Mildew on Siding: A Complete Removal Guide
heroIntro: Black speckles, green film, and dark streaks under the eaves are organic growth, not dirt. Here is how to clean it off without damaging the siding, and why painting over it never works.
excerpt: Black streaks and green film on siding are living growth. How to identify it, clean it safely, and stop it coming back in Florida humidity.

keywords.primary: how to remove mold from siding

Why does mold keep coming back on the north side of my house?

sections.h2: Mold, mildew, or algae? Identify what is on the wall
body: Homeowners tend to call everything "mold," but the growth on Florida siding is usually one of three things. Mildew shows up as fine black or gray speckling, often on painted trim and under soffits. Algae forms a green or yellow-green film, most often low on walls near shrubs and lawn. True mold tends to be fuzzier and darker and is most common where wood or siding stays damp. All three need the same basic treatment on the outside of a house: kill the growth, rinse it off, and remove the conditions that feed it.

A quick test separates growth from dirt. Put a few drops of diluted household bleach (roughly one part bleach to three parts water) on a cotton swab and dab a dark spot. If it lightens within a minute or two, it is organic growth. If nothing changes, you are looking at dirt, soot, or tannin bleed, which need a different cleaner. Pollen staining is its own problem; our guide to cleaning Florida pollen stains covers that.

sections.h2: Why it grows where it grows
body: Growth follows moisture and shade. The north wall, the side facing a wooded lot, and any elevation hit daily by irrigation stay wet for hours after the sun has dried everything else. In a North Central Florida summer, overnight humidity and heavy dew keep those surfaces damp almost continuously, and the film of pollen and dust on the siding gives spores something to feed on.
Look for the pattern, because it tells you what to change:
bullets: A band of green at sprinkler height means overspray is wetting the wall every morning.
Streaks under roof edges point to missing or overflowing gutters dumping water down the face.
Growth that hugs shrubs and trees means the wall never gets airflow or sun.
Black speckles across an entire older paint job often mean the coating has chalked and lost its mildewcide.

sections.h2: Cleaning siding the right way: soft washing
body: The professional method is soft washing: a low-pressure application of a cleaning solution that kills the growth at the root, followed by a gentle rinse. High pressure alone just shreds the visible top layer and leaves roots in the surface, so the stain returns within months. Worse, a pressure washer held too close can gouge wood siding, force water behind vinyl laps, etch stucco, and strip paint you wanted to keep.
For a DIY clean on a one-story wall, the process looks like this:
bullets: Pre-wet plants, grass, and any nearby surfaces you do not want treated, and cover delicate shrubs with plastic.
Mix a siding cleaner labelled for mildew, or a diluted sodium hypochlorite solution with a small amount of surfactant, following the label. Never mix bleach with ammonia or acid-based cleaners.
Apply from the bottom up with a pump sprayer or garden-hose applicator so the solution does not streak down dry siding.
Let it dwell for the time on the label, usually 5 to 15 minutes, without letting it dry on the surface.
Rinse thoroughly from the top down with low pressure, then rinse the plants again.
Wear eye protection, gloves, and long sleeves, and work from the ground or a stable ladder only.

sections.h2: Repainting after mold: what has to happen first
body: Painting over mildew does not seal it in. The growth keeps living under the new film, feeds on the binder, and pushes through as gray shadows, sometimes within a single season. Before any coating goes on, the surface must be cleaned with a mildewcide, rinsed, and allowed to dry completely. On wood, that may take a couple of dry days; a moisture meter takes the guessing out.

Bare or chalky spots should be spot-primed with an exterior primer suited to the substrate. The topcoat should be a quality 100% acrylic exterior paint with a mildew-resistant formula. These products include biocides that slow regrowth, although they wear out over time, which is why an old paint job eventually stops resisting mildew. If the home was built before 1978, test any paint you plan to scrape or sand for lead first and follow lead-safe work practices.

Persistent growth is sometimes a symptom of water getting into the wall, not just sitting on it. If you find soft wood, swollen trim, or paint that bubbles in the same spot, read our article on hidden siding moisture damage before you repaint.
Cleaning resets the clock; changing the conditions slows it down. The highest-value fixes are cheap:
bullets: Adjust or redirect sprinkler heads so they water the lawn, not the wall.
Trim shrubs and limbs back so there is at least a foot or two of air between plants and siding.
Clean gutters and make sure downspouts discharge well away from the foundation.
Wash the house once a year, ideally in spring after the pollen season, before summer humidity arrives.
Choose a mildew-resistant topcoat at the next repaint, especially on north and shaded elevations.

body: A single-story wall with light speckling is a reasonable weekend job with a pump sprayer and a garden hose. Two-story elevations, steep grades, roof-line streaking, and fragile substrates such as old wood siding or stucco are better left to a crew with soft-wash equipment and fall protection. Ladders and slick cleaning solution are a bad combination.

It also makes sense to call a professional if the paint underneath is failing, since cleaning will expose peeling and chalking that needs to be addressed anyway. faqs.q: Can I just pressure wash mold off my siding?
faqs.a: High pressure removes the visible layer but usually leaves the root system behind, so the stain returns quickly. It can also damage wood, vinyl, and stucco. A low-pressure soft wash with a mildew-killing solution is the safer and longer-lasting method.

faqs.q: Is mold on exterior siding dangerous?
faqs.a: Surface mildew and algae on the outside of a house are mainly a cosmetic and maintenance problem, but they hold moisture against the surface and shorten paint life. If growth is accompanied by soft wood, bubbling paint, or musty smells inside, have the wall checked for water intrusion.

faqs.q: How often should I wash my house in Florida?
faqs.a: Once a year is a good baseline for most homes in North Central Florida, with shaded or heavily irrigated walls sometimes needing attention more often. Spring, after the heavy pollen season, is a practical time to do it.

faqs.q: Will mildew-resistant paint stop growth completely?
faqs.a: No paint stops growth permanently. Mildew-resistant exterior coatings slow it down considerably, but the walls still need occasional washing and the moisture sources still need to be controlled.
